_meta.purpose: Canonical index registry. This is the JOIN KEY between a US-domiciled holding and its non-US-situs alternative. Discovery happens here, on index identity; return statistics only VERIFY a match, never discover one. Correlation is deliberately not used as a matching mechanism -- every US large-cap equity ETF correlates above 0.98 with every other one, so correlation cannot distinguish an S&P 500 tracker from a Nasdaq-100 tracker and would return confident wrong answers.

field_notes.label: Display name of the index.
field_notes.provider: Index provider. Two indices from different providers over the same exposure (e.g. S&P 500 vs MSCI USA) are a tier-2 match, not tier-1.
field_notes.exposure: Plain-language description of what is actually owned.
field_notes.n_holdings: Approximate constituent count. A large gap in this number between two indices is the clearest signal that a swap changes the portfolio -- CRSP US Total Market holds roughly 3600 names, the S&P 500 holds 500.
field_notes.family: Indices sharing a family cover materially the same exposure and are eligible for tier-2 matching. Indices in different families are never matched.

_meta.us_content_note: us_content = fraction of the index's income that is US-source and subject to US DIVIDEND withholding. Structural, set once here so the swap engine never restates it. Bond indices are set to zero: US-source INTEREST paid to a foreign fund is largely exempt under the US portfolio-interest exemption, the same reasoning already applied in cma.json. Estimates, not measured holdings weights.
_meta.withholding_divergence_from_cma: This feature does NOT use cma.json's tax.us_div_withholding.by_domicile table, which records LU at 0.15. Luxembourg UCITS generally do NOT obtain the treaty rate -- Limitation-on-Benefits clauses mean most pay the full 30 per cent, which is a principal reason Irish domicile dominates for US equity exposure. The swap engine derives the rate from the ISIN prefix instead: IE 0.15, everything else 0.30. The cma.json entry is latent rather than live (every LU fund in the deployed universe has zero US content, so the drag is zero either way) but it is wrong and is flagged for correction.
_meta.split_note: The 'semiconductors' and 'us_dividend_growers' keys each covered several genuinely different indices and were producing false tier-1 matches -- SOXX (ICE) against SEMI (MSCI ACWI IMI) diverged 6.1pp a year, VYM (FTSE High Dividend Yield) against the S&P Dividend Aristocrats lines 4.4pp. Both are now split, so cross-index pairs surface as tier-2 with a caveat instead of as exact matches. Found by the return-verification pass, not by inspection.

near_families._note: Tier-2 matching across families. Same-family pairs are close substitutes; the pairs below are NOT, and each carries the reason the swap changes the portfolio. The match engine must surface the caveat verbatim alongside any tier-2 result -- an unexplained tier-2 match is the failure mode where someone swaps a total-market holding for a large-cap one and never learns they dropped 3,100 companies.

pairs.caveat: No UCITS fund tracks a US total-market index. The nearest available exposure is US large-cap, which holds roughly 500 to 600 companies against the total market's 3,500. You keep about 85 per cent of the market capitalisation and lose the small-cap tail entirely.

No UCITS fund tracks the MSCI all-cap US technology index. The alternatives below track the S&P 500's technology slice instead: roughly 70 large-cap companies against 321, from a different index provider. You keep the mega-caps that dominate both and lose the mid- and small-cap technology tail.

No UCITS fund tracks the broad US real-estate sector. The nearest available exposure is dividend-screened — it holds US property companies that also pass a yield test, which is a narrower and income-tilted selection rather than the sector itself.

No UCITS fund tracks the FTSE Global All Cap index. The nearest available exposure is the FTSE All-World series, which holds roughly 4,300 large and mid-cap companies against the all-cap index's 8,000 -- the same countries and the same provider, without the small-cap tail.

No UCITS fund tracks the FTSE all-cap emerging series. The nearest available exposure is the large/mid FTSE Emerging Index, which holds about 2,289 companies against the all-cap index's 4,852 -- the same countries and the same provider, without the small-cap tail. Both exclude South Korea, which FTSE classifies as developed.
A US small-cap holding swapped into a total-market or large-cap line is not a substitute -- it removes the small-cap tilt that was the point of the position.

The Nikkei 225 is PRICE-weighted, not capitalisation-weighted. A handful of high-priced shares dominate it in a way they do not dominate a capitalisation-weighted Japan index, so this is a different portfolio rather than a cheaper wrapper around the same one.
